lessonTitle: Strain Gauge Measurement and Bridge Circuits

blocks.text: A wind-turbine blade in a test hall is bent by hydraulic rams while a few dozen strain gauges, each a foil grid the size of a postage stamp, stretch and squeeze with the blade skin. The change in a gauge's resistance is only about 0.1%, so to read it the gauge is wired into a Wheatstone bridge that turns a tiny resistance change into a measurable voltage.

blocks.markdown: An electrical resistance **strain gauge** is a metal foil grid bonded to a surface. When the surface strains by $\varepsilon$, the gauge strains with it and its resistance $R$ changes by $\Delta R/R=\mathrm{GF}\,\varepsilon$, where the **gauge factor** $\mathrm{GF}$ (typically about 2.0 for metal foil) is supplied by the manufacturer. Because $\Delta R/R$ is of order $10^{-3}$, gauges are connected as arms of a **Wheatstone bridge**, whose output voltage $V_{out}$ is proportional to the strain and to the **excitation voltage** $V_{ex}$ (V). We assume equal nominal resistances in all four arms, small strains ($\varepsilon\ll1$) and negligible lead-wire effects.

blocks.caption: Bridge output for a single active gauge in a bridge with four equal arms, small strain

blocks.title: Bridge configurations
blocks.text: In a **quarter bridge** one arm is an active gauge and the other three are fixed resistors. In a **half bridge** two arms (adjacent arms) are active. In a **full bridge** all four arms are active gauges. Gauges in adjacent arms subtract their effects, while gauges in opposite arms add.

blocks.title: Strain from bridge output (quarter bridge)
blocks.prompt: A single active gauge ($\mathrm{GF}=2.10$) in a quarter bridge with $V_{ex}=5.0$ V produces $V_{out}=1.05$ mV on a steel member ($E=200$ GPa). Find the strain and stress.

blocks.markdown: **Temperature effects.** A change in temperature causes an **apparent strain** because the gauge resistance changes with temperature and because the gauge and specimen expand differently. In a quarter bridge this appears as strain that is not real. In a **bending** test, a half bridge with one gauge on the tension face and one on the compression face, placed in **adjacent arms**, has equal apparent strains from temperature which cancel in the bridge (since adjacent arms subtract), whereas the bending strains are equal and opposite and add. The sensitivity is also doubled.

blocks.title: Temperature compensation in a bending test
blocks.prompt: A steel cantilever has gauges ($\mathrm{GF}=2.0$) at the top and bottom surfaces at the same section. The true bending strain is $\pm500\ \mu\varepsilon$ and $V_{ex}=10$ V. The apparent thermal strain is $12\ \mu\varepsilon$ per K and the beam warms by 10 K. Compare a quarter bridge and a half bridge.

steps.text: Apparent strain from the temperature rise.
Quarter bridge, top gauge only: the indicated strain includes the apparent strain.
Half bridge, adjacent arms: output depends on the difference of the two gauge strains.
Output voltages for the true strain.

blocks.answer: The half bridge gives 5.0 mV (double the 2.5 mV from a quarter bridge) and no temperature error; the quarter bridge reads 24% high.

blocks.markdown: **Uncertainty.** Every measurement has an uncertainty. Contributions we treat as independent include **calibration** (the shunt-calibration or amplifier gain), the **gauge factor tolerance**, and **noise** in the signal. Each is expressed as a standard uncertainty $u_i$ (in $\mu\varepsilon$); a tolerance quoted as $\pm a$ with no further information is treated as a rectangular distribution with $u=a/\sqrt3$. Independent contributions combine in quadrature, and the **expanded uncertainty** with coverage factor $k=2$ (about 95% confidence) is $U=2u_c$.

blocks.caption: Combined standard uncertainty and expanded uncertainty

blocks.title: Uncertainty in a strain reading
blocks.prompt: A strain reading is 800 $\mu\varepsilon$. Calibration uncertainty is 0.5% of reading, gauge factor uncertainty is 1.0% of reading (both treated as standard uncertainties here) and noise is 2.0 $\mu\varepsilon$ rms. Find the combined and expanded uncertainty.
blocks.answer: Strain $=800\pm18$ $\mu\varepsilon$ (95% confidence); the gauge factor dominates the uncertainty.

items: Identify the bridge configuration and the corresponding output relation.
Convert the output voltage to strain using $\mathrm{GF}$ and $V_{ex}$, then to stress using Hooke's law.
Choose adjacent-arm active gauges to cancel temperature effects in bending.
List independent uncertainty sources, combine in quadrature and state the coverage factor.

blocks.title: Common slips
blocks.text: Using $\mathrm{GF}\varepsilon V_{ex}$ without the factor of $1/4$ for a quarter bridge; placing the compensating gauge in an **opposite** arm (which adds, not cancels, the temperature effect); and adding uncertainties linearly rather than in quadrature.

blocks.title: Design the bridge to do the work
blocks.text: Choose the gauge arrangement so that the quantity you want adds (bending strain) and the quantity you do not want subtracts (temperature, axial load in a bending test).

points: Gauge resistance changes as $\Delta R/R=\mathrm{GF}\varepsilon$; a quarter-bridge output is $V_{out}=\mathrm{GF}\,\varepsilon\,V_{ex}/4$, a half bridge doubles it and a full bridge gives $\mathrm{GF}\varepsilon V_{ex}$ in bending.
Adjacent-arm gauges cancel common effects such as temperature; opposite-arm gauges add.
A top and bottom half bridge in bending is temperature-compensated and doubles sensitivity.
Combine independent uncertainty contributions in quadrature and report an expanded uncertainty ($k=2$).

questions.stem: A single active gauge in a quarter bridge (equal resistors, small strains) with gauge factor GF and excitation $V_{ex}$ has output $V_{out}$. The strain is

distractorRationale.b: Omits the factor of 4 of the quarter bridge (this applies to the full bridge).
distractorRationale.c: Multiplies by GF instead of dividing.
distractorRationale.d: This applies to a half bridge, not a quarter bridge.

questions.explanation: The bridge output for one active arm is a quarter of the arm's fractional resistance change times $V_{ex}$. Solving for the strain gives $\varepsilon=4V_{out}/(\mathrm{GF}V_{ex})$.

questions.stem: A quarter bridge with a gauge of $\mathrm{GF}=2.0$ and $V_{ex}=10$ V is used to measure a strain of $600\ \mu\varepsilon$. The expected output is

distractorRationale.a: Omits the divide-by-four and uses $\mathrm{GF}\varepsilon V_{ex}$, which is the full bridge.
distractorRationale.c: Divides by 10 instead of 4, a slip in handling the excitation.
distractorRationale.d: This is the half-bridge value for the same strain.

questions.explanation: The quarter-bridge output is $\mathrm{GF}\varepsilon V_{ex}/4$, so $V_{out}=2.0\times6\times10^{-4}\times10/4=3\times10^{-3}$ V.

questions.stem: A quarter bridge has $V_{ex}=5.0$ V, $\mathrm{GF}=2.12$ and measures an output of 0.85 mV on a loaded member. Find the strain in microstrain ($\mu\varepsilon$).
In a cantilever bending test, which gauge arrangement cancels the effect of a uniform temperature change while increasing sensitivity?

options.text: A quarter bridge with a single gauge on the tension face
A half bridge with both gauges on the tension face in adjacent arms
A half bridge with one gauge on the tension face and one on the compression face, in adjacent bridge arms
A half bridge with the tension and compression gauges in opposite arms

questions.correctOptionText: A half bridge with one gauge on the tension face and one on the compression face, in adjacent bridge arms

distractorRationale.a: A quarter bridge has no compensation and a lower output.
distractorRationale.b: Two tension gauges in adjacent arms would cancel the bending signal, not the temperature effect.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: bending strains add (equal and opposite in adjacent arms) and temperature effects cancel.
distractorRationale.d: Opposite arms add the temperature effect rather than cancelling it, and in opposite arms equal and opposite strains would also cancel the bending signal.

questions.explanation: Adjacent arms subtract. Top and bottom gauges see equal and opposite bending strain, so the difference doubles the signal, while the common apparent thermal strain subtracts to zero.

questions.stem: A full bridge with four active gauges on a bending beam (two on the tension face, two on the compression face, wired for maximum output) has $\mathrm{GF}=2.1$, $V_{ex}=5.0$ V and a bending strain of magnitude $450\ \mu\varepsilon$. Find the output voltage in mV.
questions.explanation: For a full bending bridge, $V_{out}=\mathrm{GF}\varepsilon V_{ex}=2.1\times450\times10^{-6}\times5.0=4.725$ mV. This is four times the quarter-bridge value and it is temperature-compensated.

questions.stem: A quarter bridge ($\mathrm{GF}=2.10$, $V_{ex}=5.0$ V) indicates $V_{out}=0.88$ mV after the specimen warmed by 8 K. The combination of gauge and specimen has an apparent thermal strain of $15\ \mu\varepsilon$ per K. Find the true mechanical strain in microstrain.
questions.explanation: The indicated strain is $4(0.88\times10^{-3})/(2.10\times5.0)=335.2$ $\mu\varepsilon$. The apparent strain is $15\times8=120$ $\mu\varepsilon$, so the true strain is $335.2-120=215.2$ $\mu\varepsilon$.

questions.stem: A strain measurement has independent standard uncertainties of 3 $\mu\varepsilon$ from calibration, 4 $\mu\varepsilon$ from noise and 6 $\mu\varepsilon$ from the gauge factor tolerance. Find the combined standard uncertainty in $\mu\varepsilon$.
questions.explanation: Independent contributions add in quadrature: $u_c=\sqrt{3^2+4^2+6^2}=\sqrt{61}=7.81$ $\mu\varepsilon$. A linear sum (13 $\mu\varepsilon$) would overstate the uncertainty.

questions.stem: A strain reading is $600\ \mu\varepsilon$. The calibration uncertainty is 0.4% of reading (standard uncertainty), the gauge factor is quoted as $\pm1.0\%$ with no distribution stated, and the noise is $3.0\ \mu\varepsilon$ rms. Evaluate the combined standard uncertainty and the expanded uncertainty ($k=2$), and state which source dominates.
markingGuide: Expanded: $U=2u_c=10.3$ $\mu\varepsilon$, i.e. about 1.7% of the reading.
questions.explanation: Independent contributions combine as the square root of the sum of squares, and a bare tolerance is treated as a rectangular distribution, which divides it by $\sqrt3$. The largest contributor, here the gauge factor, sets the overall uncertainty.

questions.stem: Explain why a half bridge with gauges on the top and bottom faces of a beam (adjacent arms) gives temperature compensation and twice the output of a quarter bridge. Say what would happen if the two gauges were instead placed in opposite arms.
markingGuide: Bending strain is equal and opposite on the two faces, and bridge arms adjacent to each other subtract: the two signals add, doubling the output.
A uniform temperature change gives the same apparent strain in both gauges (same material, same $\Delta T$), so the equal changes in adjacent arms cancel.
Output $=\mathrm{GF}\varepsilon V_{ex}/2$ compared with $\mathrm{GF}\varepsilon V_{ex}/4$ for a quarter bridge.
In opposite arms the contributions add: the equal-and-opposite bending signals would cancel and the temperature signals would add, the opposite of what is wanted.
questions.explanation: The bridge responds to the difference between adjacent arms and the sum of opposite arms. Arranging bending to appear as a difference and temperature as a common signal makes the bridge sensitive to the first and blind to the second.

questions.stem: True or false: for a quarter bridge with equal arm resistances and small strains, the output voltage is proportional to the excitation voltage, so doubling $V_{ex}$ doubles $V_{out}$ for the same strain.
questions.explanation: The relation is $V_{out}=\mathrm{GF}\,\varepsilon\,V_{ex}/4$, linear in $V_{ex}$. In practice $V_{ex}$ is limited by the self-heating of the gauge, which causes drift, so it cannot be raised without limit.
